div.p: In this paper, we propose a set of scheduling procedures f o r dealing with the sporadic task scheduling in a dynamic periodic system. For this we mean a system in which periodic tasks change their parameters dynamically at run-time), in an unpredictable ent from the current periodic task set. It means that the task schedulability tests in such systems have t o be made on-line. On the other hand, on-line evaluations in Hard Real-Time Systems must be done in a fast way, once the overhead incurred in these evaluations may jeopardize the tasks timing requirements. A s it is common that exact tests, providing necessary and sufficient conditions for validatin the schedule, are intractable algoritms(EXPTIME1 they can not support on-line decisions. Then, our goal is to provide a sufficient condition f o r on-line scheduling tests which is fast(PTIME) and can be reasonably useful compared t o the exact condition. We present a series of simulation runs tha: confirm the usefulness of our approach.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Real-Time Scheduling Theory has been an important research area in the last years, since through this theory one can assure that a task set will meet its timing requirements. This work is related to the stablishment of conditions for successfully scheduling tasks. These conditions are expressed through the schedulability tests, which answers if a particular task set is schedulable in a given computer configuration using a particular scheduling algorithm. Depending on the system environment, such tests may be either fast (Liu and Layland 1973), meaning that they can be carried on-line, or they may be expensive (Leung and Merril 1980), requiring an off-line evaluation, if applied to Hard Real-Time Systems.

The questions we have mentioned above regard periodic and sporadic task sets. Periodic tasks represents the sampling and processing of data from time to time. The system also requires processes which request service in an unpredictable time, named sporadic tasks (Mok 1983 . Schedulability test for sporadic tasks is, most o 1 the time, a computationally way. So, the off-f m e periodic task set will be differ-'Supported by FAPESP-92/3507-0 Faculdade de Engenharia Elktrica Universidade Estadual de Campinas P.O. Box 6162 Campinas, SP, 13083 -Brazil expensive procedure. For Hard Real-Time Systems, run-time algorithms must be carefully designed in or- der to cope with the stringent timing requirements of Hard Real-Time tasks. This makes on-line processing of EXPTIME procedures out of question. Some applications will require a dynamic system, in a sense that periodic tasks may change their timing parameters in reaction to the environment. In air traffic control systems, for instance, we may have creation and destruction of periodic tasks. Besides, some tasks can change its own parameters, like computation and period time (Kuo and Mok 1991). In these systems, even the periodic task schedulability has to be tested on-line (Xu and Parnas 1991). As pointed before, Hard Real-Time Systems require that on-line scheduling tests must be made fast enough in order to keep the timing requirements of tasks. Based on these requirements, we present a fast sufficient condition for scheduling a sporadic task system in such a dynamic environment. We make an assumption that guaranteed periodic tasks will have priority over arriving tasks, either periodic or sporadic. We compare our results with a methodology that leads to a necessary and sufficient condition for the scheduling at expenses of more computational time (Chetto and Chetto 1989). In order to apply the off-line approach, we must have a complete system knowledge, i.e., the system must be known at pre-run-time and task parameters are not allowed to change. When applications require that periodic tasks change their parameters, this pre-runtime knowledge is lost. So, on-line approach is more suitable for these cases, since the schedulability tests take place at the moment it is needed and mirror the current system conditions.

The problem consists in determining whether one sporadic task can be scheduled in a periodic task system that is guaranteed to meet its timing requirements. If this periodic task set is known in advance (pre-run-time) and is supposed to be static, several proposals have been made, all assuming preemptive scheduling for all tasks and using priority assignment based on the Earliest Deadline.

Some review relating off-line scheduling is presented in section 2. In section 3, we present two models for the on-line schedulability test. The simulation results are discussed in section 4. Finally, the conclusion and further remarks follow in section 5 .

div.head: Off-line Methodology
div.p: This section is an overview of the conditions presented in previous works, regarding the scheduling of sporadic tasks. The problem consists in determining whether one sporadic task can be scheduled in a periodic task system that is guaranteed to meet its timing requirements. This periodic task set is known in advance (pre-run-time) and is supposed to be static. We assume preemptive scheduling for all tasks and our priority assignment is based on the Earliest Deadline, since it is an optimal policy for the conditions considered here (Liu and Layland 1973).

We consider the scheduling of a single sporadic task is the relative deadline and we assume tacitly that the deadline of each task instance is due to the next request, requiring the dpi = ppi. Through this off-line algorithm, the schedulability can be determined and if the set is schedulable, an on-line algorithm can be construted to schedule successfully the sporadic set.

div.p: In a sense to provide a complete scheduling test, we turn our attention to another transformation of sporadic tasks into periodic ones (Baruah, Mok and Rosier 1990). In this approach, a finite legal request set derived of sporadic task requests is built such that the sporadic task system is feasible iff it can be scheduled regarding to this particular task request set.

The difference between both approaches lies meaningly in the fact that the former allows the determination of sufficient condition for the sporadic task scheduling, while the later provides both sufficient and necessary conditions to do so. In terms of schedulability, both approaches rely on a static environment in order to apply their results. For instance, it is known that for these approaches, the best solution can run in pseudo-polynomial time.

div.head: Maximum Idle Time approach
div.p: According to the exact condition presented here, we need to evaluate the maximum idle time in the interval of T, valid execution, in order to decide the scheduling question(Chett0 and Chetto 1989). This amount can be obtained through a procedure that, in the mentioned interval, takes into account the total time of idle CPU and the maximum delay that can be applied to the periodic instances so that they still can meet their deadlines. This is equivalent to execute a sporadic task in this interval with computation time equal to this idle time.

div.head: Slot List scheduling
div.p: Given a periodic task set rp, we build a data structure named Slot List (SL for short), which is composed of elements that are intervals where the CPU is busy, considering the EDS policy applied to the set rp (Schwan and Zhou 1992).

The required schedulability test is performed based on the Earliest Deadline priority assignment applied at the task T, and a subset of previously scheduled tasks that contains those tasks whose scheduling conflict with the T, scheduling interval. This means that the size of the subset depends on T, interval, namely r ,,r ,+ d ,] . If any instance in the subset is unschedu-i able, T, is not accepted; otherwise it is accepted. The task subset to be rescheduled is determined using the Slot List that must be available at the time of T, arrival.

div.head: On-line methodologies for sporadic task scheduling
div.p: We previously have briefly presented some main ideas regarding sporadic task scheduling, found in the literature. All work done in this subject share the as- sumption that the periodic task set is static. Now, we must face the possibility that the periodic tasks change their parameters as a result of the particular application. In this case, we have to find a procedure that takes into account these changes, represented by new values of computation time and period for the tasks. Our objective is to find out a useful test fast enough to accomplish the job of answering if a given sporadic task is feasible in a system like this. By useful, we mean that our condition behaves in several cases quite as good as the exact condition.

div.head: Exact Condition
div.p: For some dynamic periodic task systems, it may happen that the sufficient condition described above is not very suitable, since its outcome may be poor. This is the case when the sporadic task deadline is too small and at the same time, the system is heavily loaded, leading too high values for R. On the other hand, the exact condition may not be available by hand if a dynamic changes has occured recently. This poses a difficulty in using the sufficient condition and One way to allow an exact schedulability test for T, comes &om the schedule examination generated by some scheduling policy over the tasks of the system (Schwan and Zhou 1992). For instance, the arrival of a sporadic task T, at time T , in a system with a schedulable periodic task set rP recently updated can be analysed as long as we construct a schedule for rp and T, from T, and verify if the deadlines of all instances are met, until some termination criteria. Unfortunately, the schedule construction generally leads to an intractable procedure, unless we bound the schedule size. The steps for testing the schedulability are:

For each instance j of a periodic task, we define the lateness L ( j ) as the amount of possible delay instance allowed, provided that the deadline is met. Being o ( j ) the deadline and E ( j ) the time completion of this instance, according to some scheduling policy, the lateness is defined as L ( j ) = D ( j ) -E ( j ) . If the lateness of j is non-negative, the instance can be delayed at most by this value. However, a negative lateness indicates a missing deadline. Of course, we want to guarantee that the lateness of all instances are nonnegative. Basically, the procedure will schedule instances through the optimal Earliest Deadline policy including T, , assuming that the T, highest possible value computation time is the maximum idle time in the interval [r,, r, + d,].

Our objective is to save an amount of time in the interval [ p a , r, + d,] executing only the instances that have a deadline prior to or equal r, + d , . All instances that have deadlines after r, + d , will have their executions delayed such that they start after r, + d,. This is just the implementation of the Earliest Deadline policy takin the T, maximum value computation in the interval fr,, r, + d,], postponing the executions of the instances that have deadlines greater than r, + d , such that their executions will resume no earlier than r, + d,. It should be noticed that these delayed instances are not guaranteed to meet their deadlines for such T, computation. In this case, we may have negative lateness for such instances. In order to overcome this situation, whenever we find a negative lateness instance, we decrease the proposed T, computation until the mentioned lateness becomes zero. Proceeding this way for all instances, we get the maximum T, computation that allows a successfully schedule construction.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Through the simulation shown, we see that our sufficient condition can be a very interesting measure in order to guarantee the scheduling of sporadic tasks in an environment that changes its conditions dynamically.

It is known that most sporadic tasks have computation times which are significantly smaller than their deadlines. This fact heavily contributes in favor of using this approach, specially when the number of active sporadic tasks is not large.
